case_study_insert.main_stem: Aldermere Packaging Cooperative (APC) is a cooperative in the packaging sector, manufacturing corrugated and eco-friendly cardboard boxes at high volume for e-commerce and retail fulfilment clients across the country, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Rosa Jiménez, APC operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. APC plans to invest $980,000 in an automated die-cutting and folding line, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $310,000 a year, a variable cost of $1.10 a unit and a selling price of $4.20, and currently produces 160,000 units a year. APC faces an operational problem: offcut waste has risen to 11% of output.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Waste and Quality Report — Q3 2025: APC produced 42,000 boxes last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 3.9% a year ago. Offcut waste was 11% of output, costing $26,000 in scrap last quarter. Average delivery lead time is 2.4 days. A survey of 250 e-commerce customers found 71% now specify 100% recyclable boxes, and 49% would pay $0.15 more per box. On-time fulfilment to distribution centres runs at 97%. On-the-job training is in place, but 18 of 60 members have not completed training on the new die-cutting line; off-the-job training courses cost $800 per member.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Aldermere Packaging Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $11.85 to $12.50 per hour from April 2027. (3) Recycled paper and pulp input costs have risen 13.8% year-on-year, packaging price inflation is running at 7.4%, while e-commerce packaging demand grew 6.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: APC plans to finance part of its automated die-cutting and folding line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for APC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs APC nothing in interest or repayments, which matters for a cooperative whose members share any surplus and who want stable returns. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 13.8% rise in recycled paper and pulp input costs, helping APC hold the $4.20 price for e-commerce clients and protect the $3.10 contribution per box earned on 160,000 units a year.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk attached to a bank loan, so the $380,000 does not put the new $980,000 die-cutting line at risk of repossession if demand from distribution centres falters. It also preserves the members' democratic ownership and control, since no lender can impose conditions on how the line is staffed, scheduled or priced. It also signals financial discipline to members who vote on major commitments, reinforcing trust in Rosa Jiménez's judgement. This suits APC's flat structure, where members expect a voice in big decisions and are already engaged in tackling the 11% offcut waste problem.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Aldermere Packaging Cooperative and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: APC is launching its 100% recyclable box range. Consider a social media campaign aimed at e-commerce brands, advertising in packaging trade journals, or exhibiting at an e-commerce packaging trade fair. Which should APC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media campaign: A targeted social media campaign aimed at e-commerce brands and fulfilment buyers is cheap, measurable and fast. APC can showcase the 71% of surveyed customers who specify 100% recyclable boxes and the 49% willing to pay $0.15 more, reach procurement staff precisely, and direct them to samples within days. It suits a 60-member cooperative with limited marketing budget, though results compound slowly and require consistent content and follow-up.

Packaging trade journals: Journal advertising builds credibility among packaging engineers and print buyers with repetition across issues at low cost, and it reaches an exactly relevant audience. Readership is passive, response is difficult to measure, and print lead times blunt the launch of a range tied to a 6.2% growth in e-commerce packaging demand.

Trade fair exhibition: Exhibiting puts APC's die-cut samples directly into the hands of distribution-centre buyers, supports live demonstrations of the new automated line and can win multi-year contracts on the spot. Stand space, travel and staffing are expensive, however, and one event provides only a brief window to reach the 250 e-commerce customers already surveyed.

Recommendation: APC should choose a social media campaign aimed at e-commerce brands, supported by one trade fair each year for relationship building. It delivers the widest reach per dollar, speaks directly to the 71% sustainability-first segment and reinforces APC's eco-friendly positioning at the 97% on-time fulfilment that e-commerce buyers demand. Journal advertising is rejected as too passive and slow, and exhibiting alone is rejected as too expensive and infrequent for a cooperative funding a $980,000 automated line with a $600,000 bank loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of APC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of APC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and exhibition-only approaches are rejected.

questions.question_text: APC's offcut waste has risen to 11% of output, costing $26,000 in scrap last quarter. Explain two benefits for APC of using democratic leadership to involve its members in reducing waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives APC's 60 members a genuine voice in how boxes are nested, cut and folded, which builds ownership and motivation. Members who help redesign cutting layouts are far more likely to follow new waste procedures consistently, directly attacking the 11% offcut waste rate and protecting the margin on every one of the 160,000 units produced each year. Members also learn cost-awareness, linking waste reduction to the cooperative's surplus share.

Point 2: Involving members in decisions surfaces practical, floor-level suggestions from the people who handle every sheet of corrugated board daily, improving cutting patterns and reducing the 2.6% defect rate further. Higher involvement also raises commitment and lowers the risk of members drifting away to rival plants, protecting output of 42,000 boxes last quarter and keeping scrap costs below the $26,000 recorded, so the new die-cutting line delivers its full payoff for e-commerce clients. Weekly member briefings and a public suggestion board make this involvement practical rather than ceremonial.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to APC's waste, quality and cooperative culture.

questions.question_text: APC must upskill 18 members to operate the new die-cutting line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an external centre. Which should APC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training members beside experienced cutters on the new line is directly relevant to APC's exact board grades and die layouts, costs nothing in course fees and keeps boxes flowing while members learn, protecting the 42,000-unit quarter and the 97% on-time fulfilment record. Drawbacks are that senior members lose productive time as trainers, inconsistent coaching can reinforce careless cutting and worsen the 11% offcut waste, and formal certification is limited when e-commerce clients request evidence.

Off-the-job training: External courses at $800 per member cost $14,400 for the 18 staff - affordable beside the $980,000 investment - and give structured, standardised instruction plus certificates clients can verify. However, members are removed from the floor for days at a time, squeezing output at a time when orders grew 6.2%, and generic content may not match APC's exact machines, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: APC should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with off-the-job courses reserved for three senior members who can certify competence internally. This keeps output stable, costs far less than $14,400 and fixes waste at the point where it occurs. APC should review offcut waste and defect data monthly, and shift any remaining members onto external courses once the new line stabilises and orders grow. Member feedback should shape the final training mix, consistent with APC's flat democratic culture. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because removing 18 of only 60 members during a launch financed by a $600,000 bank loan would strain delivery promises to distribution centres and delay the benefits of the automated die-cutting line.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to APC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of APC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of APC with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, waste and client certification needs.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how APC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $310,000 ÷ ($4.20 − $1.10) = $310,000 ÷ $3.10 = 100,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 100,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $4.20 − $1.10 = $3.10. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.10.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways APC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 100,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 160,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 60,000 units, judging how close the cooperative could run to break-even before the new die-cutting line becomes a problem.
2. Contribution per unit of $3.10 lets APC model a premium for 100% recyclable boxes; adding the $0.15 premium customers say they will pay raises contribution to $3.25, quantifying the gain from the market research finding that 49% accept a higher price.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $310,000 and contribution per unit helps members check that the $600,000 bank loan for the $980,000 line can be serviced before committing to further member borrowing or retained profit.
4. Managers can use average total cost ($310,000 ÷ 160,000 units + $1.10 = $3.04 a unit) to benchmark each quarter, link it to the 11% offcut waste problem and renegotiate recycled paper and pulp supply as input costs rise 13.8%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 100,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.10 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 60,000 units versus 160,000-unit output; pricing and premium modelling for recyclable boxes; loan-repayment feasibility for the $980,000 die-cutting line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $3.04 to tackle 11% offcut waste and 13.8% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate APC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has APC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.74 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.34 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $285,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $150,000 + $85,000 = $305,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $285,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $305,000 ÷ $175,000 = 1.74. Cover excluding inventories 2024 = ($285,000 − $95,000) ÷ $190,000 = $190,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.00; 2025 = ($305,000 − $70,000) ÷ $175,000 = $235,000 ÷ $175,000 = 1.34.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. Short-term cover improved from 1.50 to 1.74 as inventories were reduced from $95,000 to $70,000 and cash rose to $85,000 while liabilities eased from $190,000 to $175,000. The tougher measure excluding inventories moved from 1.00 to 1.34, so APC no longer depends on selling stock to meet short-term debts - a strong signal while it services a $600,000 bank loan for the $980,000 die-cutting line. However, trade receivables rose from $130,000 to $150,000, tying up member funds; if e-commerce clients pay late, the margin for error narrows, and inventories of $70,000 must still support timely delivery against 2.4 days lead time.

Conclusion: APC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.50 to 1.74 and 1.00 to 1.34), and the gain does not rest on stock. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so APC should tighten credit terms with distribution centres and keep monitoring the 97% on-time fulfilment rate while the new line beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether APC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for APC of switching its boxes to 100% recycled materials.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: 100% recyclable materials match the 71% of surveyed e-commerce customers who now specify recyclable boxes and the 49% willing to pay $0.15 more per box, allowing APC to defend the $4.20 selling price and lift contribution per unit above $3.10. The switch also strengthens APC's eco-friendly brand with buyers prioritising sustainability, supports marketing to the e-commerce segment growing at 6.2%, and reinforces the cooperative's environmental mission for its 60 members. It also strengthens APC's position when distribution centres audit suppliers for environmental compliance.

Disadvantage: Recycled pulp costs have risen 13.8% year-on-year and recycled fibres can be weaker or less consistent, raising the variable cost above $1.10 a unit and risking higher defect rates beyond the current 2.6%. If shelf strength or print quality fails in transit to distribution centres, APC could face claims, higher scrap beyond the $26,000 lost last quarter, and damage to the 97% on-time fulfilment reputation that anchors its e-commerce contracts. APC should trial recycled board on one product line before converting the whole 160,000-unit range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to APC's research data, materials costs and reputation.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.8% rise in input costs will affect APC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): APC's $600,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, rises by 0.75%, adding about $4,500 a year to interest costs and slightly lifting the pressure on the $310,000 fixed-cost base. Higher rates may also make members more cautious about further borrowing for the $980,000 die-cutting line. The direct impact is the smallest of the three and can be capped by fixing part of the loan.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.50 per hour): Most of APC's 60 members work on the floor near minimum wage. A rise from $11.85 to $12.50 moves each full-time member up $1,300 a year; and if we assume 50 floor members, that is roughly $65,000 a year, a direct hit to a cooperative that shares surplus among members, and a rise that may exceed the gain from the $0.15 eco premium on 160,000 boxes a year.

Input cost inflation (13.8% recycled paper and pulp): Pulp dominates the $1.10 variable cost at roughly $0.70 per box. A 13.8% rise adds about $0.10 per unit; at 160,000 units that is roughly $15,800 a year, eroding the $3.10 contribution per unit and squeezing margins on contracts with distribution centres that resist price increases.

Conclusion: The 5.5% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $65,000 a year across the member-workforce, more than four times the input-cost increase, and it lands directly on a cooperative whose identity is fair pay to members, making it awkward to offset through automation alone. The input-cost rise is the second concern at roughly $15,800 a year, while the interest-rate rise costs only about $4,500 a year and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; however, APC must negotiate the $0.15 premium across its e-commerce client base and cut the 11% offcut waste to fund the wage increase without eroding member returns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to APC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on APC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of APC with a well-justified judgment that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
